I give up. I could not find a proof of this theorem, so `/work/combi_imosl_2015_c6.lean` is unchanged and still contains its `sorry`.

The statement is IMO Shortlist 2015 C6. The finite case is easy: if `S` is finite, large `n` have no odd representation at all, so they are not clean. I could not get past the infinite case.

I assumed all large `n` are clean and tried three routes:
- **Generating functions:** I wrote the odd-sum generating function as a polynomial plus `x^(N+1)/(1−x)`, then looked for a contradiction as `x → 1`. This gave consistent asymptotics and no contradiction.
- **Counting arguments:** Counting odd and even subset sums of the first `k` elements gave no contradiction either.
- **Swap pairs:** I derived that any two disjoint "swap pairs" (two disjoint sets with equal sums and opposite parity) would give two distinct odd sets with the same sum, a contradiction. This shows `S` minus a finite set has all subset sums distinct. I could not turn that into a full contradiction.

Even with the missing key idea, formalizing the argument in Lean 4 would be a very long proof.
